headline: Co-WR1 in Denver's high-volume passing game after the Miami trade.
role: Projected for roughly 113–125 targets, competing with Courtland Sutton (125 targets, 1,017 yards last season) for the team lead and clear of Troy Franklin (104). Denver has thrown ~565 times per season across two years of Payton and Nix, so even a 20% share is a real weekly floor.
fit: Widely graded a scheme match for Sean Payton. One personnel executive called it 'perfect for Sean; a good route runner who can get in and out of his breaks in the short-to-intermediate area and can also get loose deep.' Denver spent a 2026 first plus a third and a fourth to get him and owes him ~$41.2M over two years — an offense that paid that much builds him into the plan rather than rotating him.
risk: He turns 28 during the season, so this is production bought at the flat part of the WR age curve, not an appreciating dynasty asset. Sutton is still on the roster and still the incumbent, so the target crown is a competition, not a coronation.

headline: Real target vacancy in Chicago, but a three-way scramble to inherit it.
role: D.J. Moore (85 targets, 14.8% share) and Olamide Zaccheaus (11.3%) are both gone, opening roughly a quarter of the target pie. Before a Week 9 foot injury last season Odunze led the Bears in targets, red-zone looks and air-yards share while ranking top-10 in WR fantasy points per game.
fit: Positioned as the primary outside receiver in Ben Johnson's offense, and a positive-regression candidate if Caleb Williams takes the step the staff was hired to produce.
risk: The competition for those vacated targets is real: analysts say he 'could lead the 2026 Bears in targets, though he could also finish third,' with Luther Burden and tight end Colston Loveland — who looked unstoppable down the stretch — both in line for a share. Last year's production was also dragged down by the foot injury and inconsistent quarterback play.

headline: Three-down back and red-zone hammer for one of the league's best offenses.
role: Took 55.7% of Rams rush attempts to Blake Corum's 31.2%, and played 69.2% of offensive snaps to Corum's 27.8%. Critically, he held 63% of the red-zone rushing attempts — the touches that actually decide running back scoring.
fit: Beat writers expect Corum's carry share to grow toward an even split, but the split is by type, not by half: Williams stays the third-down and between-the-tackles back, Corum is the change-of-pace explosive runner. In a PPR league that division protects the valuable half of the workload — receiving work and goal-line carries stay with Williams.
risk: Corum outperformed him in nearly every non-volume metric, including a 6.9% explosive-run rate that ranked sixth among backs with 100+ carries. If McVay acts on that, the committee tilts faster than the role description suggests.

headline: Early-down workhorse in New Orleans — with the passing-down work going to Kamara.
role: Getting the bulk of first-team reps on early downs while Alvin Kamara handles third downs and passing situations, per Jeff Duncan of Nola.com. The depth chart lists them as co-starters; the practice split is the more useful fact. He is coming off 1,399 scrimmage yards and 13 touchdowns in Jacksonville, with 1,107 rushing on 260 carries, and has cleared 1,000 rushing yards in three of his four healthy seasons.
fit: Tyler Shough enters his first full season as the starter after going 5-4 with 2,256 passing yards, 10 touchdowns and five interceptions as a rookie. A young starter usually means a run-leaning script early, which points volume at the early-down back.
risk: The receiving work is the problem, not the carries. Kamara taking third downs removes the PPR half of the job, which caps the weekly ceiling in a full-PPR league no matter how many carries arrive. At 27.5 he is also a short-window asset, not a dynasty hold.

headline: Efficient young back whose touches have not arrived yet.
role: Rushed 180 times for 911 yards and nine touchdowns as a rookie at 5.1 yards per carry — eighth best among qualified backs — and caught 83% of his targets. But he played just 31.4% of offensive snaps during the playoff run, and beat writers describe a committee where Rhamondre Stevenson takes early downs and short yardage while Henderson works second- and third-and-long, contingent on his pass protection holding up.
fit: Same offense as Drake Maye, so a manager holding both watches one set of tape. If Stevenson slips or gets hurt, reporting suggests Henderson has the talent to take the job outright.
risk: A durability question sits under the profile: a severe turf-toe injury at Ohio State fractured a sesamoid bone and tore ligaments, and he re-aggravated it repeatedly in college. Combine that with an unresolved role and the range of outcomes is genuinely wide.

headline: Permanent WR2 in Cincinnati — which is still a lot of football.
role: The number-two target behind Ja'Marr Chase, but Cincinnati throws enough that the role produces WR1-caliber raw volume anyway. The cap here is positional, not situational: Chase eats first.
fit: Joe Burrow's offense is one of the league's most pass-heavy, which is what keeps a clear WR2 in weekly starter range rather than in flex purgatory.
risk: He turns 28 during the season and his ceiling is structurally limited by the receiver in front of him. For a roster that already carries a short-window veteran, he is a second bet on the same timeline rather than a diversifying one.

headline: The younger option in a top-tier offense, with only one mouth ahead of him.
role: Detroit's clear WR2 behind Amon-Ra St. Brown, in one of the league's most productive offenses. St. Brown commands volume but is not a receiver who erases everyone else's share.
fit: At 25 he is meaningfully younger than the other veteran receivers in this range, so he holds dynasty value past the current window rather than expiring with it.
risk: He missed practice in mid-August with a shoulder injury. Beat reporting called it minor and not expected to be serious, but it is an open designation rather than a clean bill of health.

headline: Young, talented, and stuck in a crowded Tampa backfield.
role: Part of a committee rather than a lead back, which is the whole case against him at this price — the talent is not in question, the touches are.
fit: Tampa's offense supports a productive back; it has not yet committed to one, and analysts repeatedly flag role security as the open question.
risk: He ranks behind Kyren Williams positionally in consensus despite being two years younger, which is the market pricing the committee risk rather than the player.

headline: The best available tight end by a wide margin — and the right way to solve a TE hole.
role: An every-down tight end in a high-scoring Detroit offense, ranked roughly 65 consensus spots ahead of the next tier of tight ends on the board.
fit: This league's +0.5 TE premium turns an every-down tight end from a luxury into a weekly structural edge, which is exactly the gap that separates him from a streaming option.
risk: He shares an offense with Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams, so the target ceiling is bounded by genuinely good teammates.

headline: A name that feels like a solution and prices like a reach.
role: Consensus has him around TE14 — not the best tight end available, and not close to it.
fit: The TE premium is real but it is +0.5, not a multiplier that turns a mid-tier tight end into an advantage. Filling the slot is not the same as winning it.
risk: Taking him where the board says a top-35 overall player belongs spends a premium pick on replacement-level production. The tight end hole is better solved later, or by trade.
